spec.name: Spitfire Mk I Blueprint
spec.description: A Supermarine Spitfire Mk I fighter in tail-down rest stance, built entirely in cyanotype blues with Prussian-blue skins, pale-blue undersides and white drafting linework picking out every panel, rivet row, control surface and roundel.
spec.layout: Real-size single-engine monoplane, nose toward +Z. The prop spinner tip is at z=4.15 and the rudder trailing edge at z=-5.0. The wings are at their widest in x (tips at x=±5.6). The fuselage axis is tilted about 4° tail-down: its centreline height is y(z)=1.40+0.07*z. From front to back: three-blade propeller disc (radius 1.5, hub on the tilted axis at [0,1.66,3.75], disc spans y≈0.16..3.16) -> pointed spinner -> deep engine cowling with six exhaust stacks per side and a chin carburettor scoop -> windscreen and sliding bubble canopy over the cockpit -> back fuselage tapering to a thin tail cone -> tailplane, fin and rudder. Elliptical low wings (6° dihedral) sit at fuselage mid-height with wing-root fillets. A radiator under each wing: oil cooler on the left, coolant radiator on the right. Two main legs splay slightly outward to the wheels (centres y=0.35, x=±0.95) and a small tail wheel sits under the rear fuselage. The wheels and the tail wheel are the only things on y=0; the prop tip clears the floor at y≈0.16. The cyanotype look comes from colour discipline, not from smooth shading. Every skin is a flat blue from the palette: upper surfaces `skin` with irregular wavy 'camouflage' patches of `skinAlt` (small flat shaped parts or sweep sectors seated on the surface), undersides and belly `skinLow` (a lighter sky blue), inner structure and shadow areas `deep`. All details are thin white or pale-blue drafting lines built as slim parts (rods or flat extrudes of radius about 0.006-0.008) in `line` or `paper`: panel seams, hatch and flap outlines, gun-port rings, rivet rows (tiny chalk studs), a fine outline along control-surface edges, tick marks, fastener rows on the cowl. Roundels are stacked flat discs or rings in roundelOuter, roundelWhite, roundelMid and roundelCore, seated on the skin with a slight offset. The serial letters and code letters are tiny blocky letter parts in `paper`. No ground, no extra scenery.

parts.builds: Everything forward of z=2.3. (1) The engine cowling: a faceted loft from the fuselage station at noseJoin (w 0.90, h 1.02, centred on the tilted axis y=1.40+0.07z) tapering to the cowl lip at z=3.5 (w 0.80, h 0.88, centre 1.645). Top and sides in `skin`, belly in `skinLow`, a `skinAlt` camouflage patch, and a `paper` cowl lip ring at the front. (2) Cowl details in `line`/`chalk`: a vertical panel seam at z=2.9, two rows of small fastener studs, and a hinged-panel outline on each side. (3) Six exhaust stacks per side, short flared tubes in `exhaust` with `deep` mouths, in a row along z 2.5..3.3 on the cowl flanks and angled back. (4) A chin carburettor scoop under the nose (z 2.4..3.2): a boxy `skinLow` scoop with a `deep` mouth and a `line` rim. (5) Two small gun-trough bulges on the top of the cowl, in `skinAlt`. (6) The pointed spinner (lathe, 8-10 sides) in `spinner`, base radius 0.28 at spinnerBase and tip at z=4.15, with a `paper` band ring near the base and `line` seam rings. (7) The propeller on joint `propeller`: a hub disc in `steel`, three blades 120° apart, each a flat tapered extruded blade of length 1.5 from the hub, with a slight twist or tilt, in `propBlade`, a `propTip` stripe at the tip, a `line` leading-edge edge and a small `chalk` root collar. The prop axis is propAxis.
parts.attaches: Cowl rear station meets the fuselage part at mount noseJoin (same w 0.90, h 1.02 at z=2.3). Spinner and propeller ride joint propeller at mount propHub. The cowl and exhausts ride joint fuselage.

parts.builds: The main body from z=2.3 back to z=-3.3. (1) A loft over the centreline y=1.40+0.07z with stations (z, width, height): 2.3 (0.90, 1.02); 1.2 (0.92, 1.12); 0.2 (0.88, 1.15); -0.8 (0.78, 1.08); -2.0 (0.62, 0.90); -3.3 (0.42, 0.66). Flat-sided with a rounded top, a keel line below, sky-blue `skinLow` on the belly and `skin` on top and sides, with irregular `skinAlt` camouflage patches seated on top. (2) The windscreen with a `glassFrame` frame and a `glass` front pane, plus a sliding bubble canopy (z 1.3..-1.2, top about y 2.28) in `glass` with `glassFrame` ribs (4 hoops and a rail along each side) and a `line` outline, on joint `canopy`. (3) A cockpit seen inside the canopy: an armoured headrest and seat in `deep`/`midBlue`, a control stick, a small round instrument panel with a `paper` dial ring, and a ring-and-bead gunsight on the coaming in `chalk`. (4) A wing-root fairing line (a `line` curve where the wing meets the fuselage at z 1.0..-1.5). (5) Fuselage roundels on both sides at z≈-2.2 (radius about 0.28: roundelOuter, roundelWhite, roundelMid and roundelCore discs), and tiny blocky code letters in `paper` forward of them. (6) Panel seams as thin `line` rods: a ring at every 0.6 m of z, a dorsal centre seam, access hatches (rectangles outlined in `line`), and rows of chalk rivets along the seams. (7) A small radio mast on top behind the canopy (z -1.5) with an aerial wire (thin `line` sweep) to the fin top at [0,2.5,-4.7]. (8) A small tail-wheel doors line and an underside fuel-tank hatch outline.
parts.attaches: Front station meets the nose part at noseJoin; rear station meets the tail part at tailJoin ([0,1.17,-3.3], w 0.42, h 0.66). Wings are seated at wingRootL/R. The canopy rides joint canopy at canopyHinge; the rest rides joint fuselage.

parts.builds: Both elliptical wings, mirrored in x, in the shape of a Spitfire wing. Per half: leading-edge and trailing-edge points at x=0.35 (z 1.0, -1.5), x=2.5 (0.65, -1.3), x=4.5 (0.0, -0.95), x=5.3 (-0.35, -0.75), tip x=5.6 (z -0.55). Wing centre height y=1.00+(|x|-0.35)*0.105 (6° dihedral), thickness 0.32 at the root to 0.08 at the tip; build it as a loft or a series of extruded slabs on the joints wingL/wingR. The top is `skin` with wavy `skinAlt` camouflage patches, the underside is `skinLow`. Separate control surfaces: an aileron on joint aileronL/R (x 3.0..5.2, rear 25% of chord) and a split flap on joint flapL/R (x 0.9..2.9, rear 25%) in `skinAlt`/`lightBlue`, each with a `paper` outline, hinge line and rib lines. Wing-root fillets blend into the fuselage in `skin`. Details: a wing roundel on each upper surface at x=±3.4, z≈-0.4 (radius 0.45: roundelOuter, roundelWhite, roundelMid and roundelCore, seated on the surface); a smaller roundel on each underside; 4 machine-gun muzzle holes per wing in a row at x 1.6..2.5 near the leading edge (little `ink` tubes with `line` rings); a gun-bay panel outline in `line`; rib seams every 0.5 m in `line` with chalk rivet rows; an under-wing radiator box at x=2.2 on the right wing (the coolant radiator, `steelDark` with a `deep` grille and `line` slats) and a rounder oil cooler at x=-3.0... mirrored: the oil cooler on the left wing at x=+3.0 and the radiator on the right at x=-2.2; a pitot tube on the left wing underside (a thin `steel` rod with a `paper` tip); a nav light bead on each tip (`paper`); a wheel-well outline on the underside near x=±0.9. Wheel-well doors are NOT part of this part.
parts.attaches: Roots sit at wingRootL/R and the fuselage sides (x=±0.35). The gear hips at gearHipL/R are under the wing at x=±0.85, z=0.3 (the wing underside is at about y=0.93 there). Ailerons and flaps ride joints aileronL/R and flapL/R; the wing skin rides wingL/R.

parts.builds: The rear cone and the tail group, z from -3.3 to -5.0. (1) The tail cone: a loft from tailJoin (w 0.42, h 0.66, centre y=1.17) through (-4.3: w 0.26, h 0.46) to (-5.0: w 0.14, h 0.28) along y=1.40+0.07z, with `skin` top and `skinLow` belly, a `paper` tail-cone cap and a `line` seam ring. (2) The fin: a flat extrude outline (pieces seated on the fuselage top at finRoot) with its leading edge from (z -3.3, y 1.35) sweeping up to (z -4.55, y 2.5), a top rounded at the rudder, thickness 0.07, in `skin`. A `line` outline and rivet rows, plus a fin-flash stripe set (roundelOuter, roundelWhite, roundelMid bands). (3) The rudder on joint `rudder`: hinge line from (z -4.5, y 1.3) to (z -4.6, y 2.45), trailing edge to z -5.0 at the bottom and about -4.95 at the top, rounded, in `skinAlt`, with a small trim tab at the trailing edge in `lightBlue`, `paper` ribs and an outline. (4) The tailplane (horizontal stabiliser): about x ±1.5, root chord 1.15 (z -3.75..-4.9), tip chord 0.4, elliptical tips, thin 0.06, at y≈1.095, with the leading edge in `skin` and elevators on joints elevatorL/R (the rear 0.35 of chord) in `skinAlt` with `paper` outlines and rib lines, and `chalk` rivets. (5) The tail wheel: a strut on joint `tailStrut` from tailStrutTop [0,0.86,-4.15] down to the axle (a `steel` rod plus a `steelDark` fork), a wheel on joint `tailWheel` at tailWheelAxle [0,0.1,-4.2], radius 0.1, width 0.06, in `tyre` with a `hub` centre; the bottom of the tyre rests on y=0. (6) Details: an underside nav-light bead (`paper`), a rear aerial anchor on the fin top, and a tail-plane bracing strut line on each side in `line`.
parts.attaches: The cone front meets the fuselage part at tailJoin. The fin sits at finRoot on the cone top; the tailplane crosses at tailplaneRoot [0,1.095,-4.35]. The rudder rides joint rudder at rudderHinge, the elevators ride elevatorL/R, the tail wheel rides tailStrut and tailWheel. The skin rides joint fuselage.

parts.builds: The main landing gear, mirrored. Per side: an oleo leg from gearHip (x=±0.85, y=0.95, z=0.3) splayed slightly outward to the wheel axle at wheel (x=±0.95, y=0.35, z=0.3): a thick `steel` upper cylinder with a thinner `paper` lower piston, a `steelDark` fork on the outboard side, a scissor torque-link (two short `line` rods meeting at a pivot bead), a brake line (thin `line` sweep), and a `deep` hinge fitting at the wing. The wheel (on joint wheelL/R, bone axis along ±x): a tyre (a chunky faceted tube/lathe, radius 0.35, width 0.16) in `tyre` with a `midBlue` sidewall band, a `hub` disc centre with `ink` bolt-circle studs (6 small studs), a `paper` hub-cap ring and `line` tread-notch ticks around the rim. A wheel-well fairing door in `skinLow` hangs on each leg (a thin flat plate along the leg's outer face, 0.5 long) with a `line` outline and rivets, and a second smaller inner door in `skin` near the fuselage. The wheel's lowest point rests on y=0.
parts.attaches: Leg tops at gearHipL/R under the wings (wing underside y≈0.93 at x=±0.85). The wheels sit at wheelL/R. The legs ride gearL/R and the wheels ride wheelL/R.

calls.reasoning:
I'm working out the Spitfire's real-world dimensions—wingspan, length, height with its elliptical wings—so the model stands correctly on the ground with the nose facing forward, and planning a cyanotype blueprint aesthetic with deep Prussian blue tones.

I'm working out the tail-down stance geometry, tilting the fuselage centerline slightly so the nose sits higher than the tail, then figuring out where the tailwheel strut meets the ground given the fuselage radius back there.

Now I'm thinking about how to split the model into manageable parts—likely separating the forward fuselage (cowling, spinner, propeller, exhausts) from the rear fuselage (canopy, headrest, aerial mast, panel lines, roundels) so each piece stays a reasonable size to construct.

Then I'm planning the wings as their own group, elliptical shape with ailerons, flaps, roundels, gun ports, underwing radiators and pitot tube, plus the tail assembly with tailplane, fin, rudder, elevators, and tail wheel, each needing their own joints so they can connect back to the fuselage properly.

For the undercarriage I'm laying out the main legs, wheels, doors, and tail wheel, keeping it to about five parts total. Even though static models don't strictly need joints, I want to treat this more like a vehicle skeleton with hinges for control surfaces -- a root joint at the fuselage spine, a hinge joint for the propeller at the spinner, hinges for ailerons, flaps, elevators, and rudder, and leg/wheel joints for the landing gear.

Now I'm working out the fuselage spine line as a function of z to place everything consistently, picking a slope that gives roughly a 4-degree rise from tail to nose, and using that to position the wing roots along the fuselage.

I'm placing the wing root leading edge near the nose-cowl region and trailing edge further back, with the wing low-mounted and a small dihedral angle so the tips sit a bit higher than the root. I'm also setting the wheel radius and figuring out where the main gear legs extend outward from the wing.

Now I'm working out the wheel track width based on the real Spitfire's 5.75 ft spacing, positioning the legs slightly splayed outward from the wing attachment down to the wheel centers, then moving on to place the tailplane further aft on the fuselage.

I'm now sizing the tail assembly—fin height, tailplane span and chord—scaling them against the real aircraft's dimensions, then checking the propeller spinner and blade radius against the fuselage centerline to make sure the prop tip clears the ground properly.

Adjusting the nose height formula, I'm balancing the overall model size so the prop tip, not the tail, sets the bounding height at 3.25, with width fixed at 11.2 (wing tips ±5.6) and length spanning from spinner to tail at roughly 9.15 units. Now I'm defining the fuselage cross-section radii at the cowl, cockpit, and tail taper points to build the loft profile.

I'll split ownership so the fuselage part lofts the main body from z=2.3 back to the tail, while the nose part handles the cowling from 2.3 to 3.55 including cowl rings, spinner, propeller, exhaust stacks, and the chin carb intake. I'm sketching station widths and heights along the fuselage, like roughly 0.90 wide by 1.00 tall near the cowl junction and about 0.92 wide at the cockpit station, to keep the two parts matching smoothly.

Continuing the nose cowl loft toward the front lip, then adding a spinner cone roughly 0.65 long tapering to a hub, tilted slightly upward along the fuselage axis to match the 4° incidence. I'm placing the propeller disc centered around z=3.75 with a blade radius of about 1.5, aligned to that same tilted axis.

Now I'm roughing out the wing planform: root chord near the fuselage edge spanning roughly 2.5 units with a leading edge further forward and a straighter trailing edge, tapering outboard into the elliptical tips characteristic of a Spitfire-style wing, extending out to about x=5.6.

I'm also working through dihedral, applying a slight upward angle from the root so the tip sits higher than the fuselage centerline, and tapering thickness from a thicker root section down to a thin tip. I'm checking that the wing root height lines up reasonably with the fuselage's lower surface so they blend without gaps.

Now I'm placing the landing gear: main legs mounted near the wing root with wheels sized and positioned so their bottoms touch the ground plane, and a smaller tail wheel further aft attached to a strut hanging from the fuselage underside.

I'm also working out the tailplane geometry—its span, root and tip chords, thickness, and vertical position relative to the fuselage—before moving on to the fin's base dimensions.

Next I'm sketching the fin and rudder outlines, placing the leading edge, trailing edge, hinge line, and top points to define their shapes, then setting the chord boundaries for the ailerons and flaps along the wing.

Now I'm working through the full joint list: defining hinge directions for the ailerons, then placing each joint's position, orientation, and role — fuselage root as the spine, the propeller hinge at the nose, and the wing root joint with its direction and role.

Still defining joint positions...

I'll split it so the tail part owns the rear cone, fin, rudder, tailplane, elevators, tail wheel, and nav light, while the fuselage keeps the main body loft, canopy, cockpit interior, panel lines, roundels, serials, and aerial mast.

Wings get both wing surfaces, ailerons, flaps, their own roundels, gun ports, underwing radiators (oil cooler on one side, radiator on the other), pitot, nav lights, and panel lines, bounded by a wing box spanning roughly x ±5.6 to z ±1.6. Then undercarriage starts with the legs, wheels, and covers.

I'm allocating a part budget: roughly 160 for the nose, 200 fuselage, 220 wings, 150 tail, 130 gear, totaling 860 out of a 900 cap, and working out the nose box dimensions with a propeller joint. I'm also starting to pick a cyanotype-inspired color palette with deep prussian blue tones for the main body.

Now I'm finalizing prop, spinner, exhaust, tyre and hub colors, plus assembling the full 24-color cyanotype palette with paper, chalk, line, and blue gradient tones.

I'm thinking through a Battle of Britain-style countershading scheme: darker two-tone blue on top surfaces versus a lighter sky blue underside, applying it as sectors across the fuselage and belly rather than a uniform tone.

Now I'm sketching the key attachment points — the cowl/fuselage seam, spinner base, propeller hub with its axis, and the wing root joints on either side — to define where parts will connect structurally.

I'm also laying out the rest: gear hips, wheels, tail join, tail tip, fin root, tailplane root, tailwheel axle, and cockpit deck points, then double-checking the fuselage cross-section dimensions at the nose to make sure the cowl front radius aligns properly before working out where the gear legs attach.

Checking the wing underside position against the gear hip to make sure the leg length and wheel placement work geometrically, and verifying the wing's dihedral curve matches across the span.

Now I'm working out the fuselage cross-section bounds through the canopy and belly region, making sure the canopy's rise stays within the fuselage height envelope, then setting up the tail section's bounding box with the floor at ground level.

Wings, radiators, landing gear, and nose boxes are falling into place, giving an overall plane length of about 9.15 units from tail to nose. I'm thinking about keeping the blueprint aesthetic consistent — everything in blue tones with thin white lines for panel seams, rivets, and outline details to sell the technical-drawing look.

Now I'm placing the roundel insignia, checking fuselage width at different z-positions to make sure a radius-0.3 circle fits proportionally on the sides without overflowing the body contour, plus considering roundel placement on the upper wing surfaces.

Writing the joint hierarchy JSON...

I'll skip the pilot figure but add cockpit details like a gunsight, seat, and stick, plus a chin intake under the nose cowl and wing root fairings to blend the wings into the fuselage. Then I'll finalize the color palette with hex values and assemble everything into the final JSON output.

I'm figuring out the buildNose function signature, destructuring the context object with joint, palette, and mount references, and deciding how to handle the Ctx type since it's not directly importable into the module.

Now I'm working through the cowl geometry — a tilted axis with a loft from the base station to the tip, varying width and height along the way, with color sectors for the dorsal and belly surfaces. I'm uncertain whether the loft function accepts options like polygon sides or sector colors directly, so I'm weighing a safer fallback approach of building the cowl manually through a sweep instead.

For surface details, I'm considering using ray-casting against the cowl surface to place rings and seams, since the cross-section is polygonal and hard to solve analytically — querying hit points along z stations to position rods and loops accurately.

For the lip ring near the nose tip, I'll place a slightly thicker swept loop close to the edge rather than a simple torus, and I'm making sure the fuselage bone is passed explicitly to all sweep operations so they ride correctly.

Now I'm working out fastener studs along both sides using rays cast inward from outside points, embedding small chalk spheres at the hit points in two offset rows, then sketching the hinged-panel outline as a rectangle drawn onto the surface and swept into rods.

Writing the seam path helper...

I'm deciding to position the hinged panel above the exhaust stacks on the cowl flanks, working out the vertical placement relative to the cowl's half-height.

That's too many parts with two rows per side at that spacing, so I'm cutting stud density down to 7 per row across 4 rows for 28 total. Tallying the part budget now: cowl, skin patches, lip and seam rings, panel outlines, studs, exhaust stacks (tube plus mouth each), scoop assembly, gun bulges, and spinner all need to fit within the 170-part limit, so I'm trimming wherever possible.

I'm also planning out exhaust stacks as short flared tubes angled back along the fuselage, placing them by raycasting outward from the flank to find surface hit points and normals, then sweeping a tapered tube from that base point angled slightly back and outward from the hull.

Setting flat caps and 6 sides for the sweep geometry, then working out the spike stack positions along the flank — placing six segments from z=2.5 to 3.3, each embedded slightly into the surface with its base offset inward along the normal, and figuring out where the hexagonal cross-section's vertices land relative to the surface height.

For the sector boundaries, I'll just pick angle ranges like 130..230 that roughly align with the octagon's faces and accept some imprecision. For the small bulges on the gun trough's top, I'm placing flattened sphere shapes at ±0.16 in x using downward surface rays to position them correctly.

For the actual bulge geometry, instead of scaled spheres I'll use capsules between two ray-hit points along the surface, sinking them slightly and giving them a small radius around 0.045.

For details, I'm adding a tiny ink-colored disc at the front of each bulge for a muzzle-like accent, and considering camouflage patches as flat extruded shapes seated directly on the surface, figuring out the local x/z plane and thickness axis for the extrusion.

Since the cowl's top is faceted into a ridge rather than flat, a draped patch there would float oddly at the edges, so I'm thinking about using angular sector patches with fromT/toT ranges instead -- essentially carving rectangular camo regions directly into the loft geometry at offset angle ranges for a more natural fit.

Alternatively, I could seat small flattened disc shapes (low-sided cylinders acting like stickers) onto the cowl's facets using embed, clustering several overlapping discs of varying radius to build up a wavy patch effect since textured decals aren't an option with flat colors only.

Adjusting for the lip exclusion zone, I'm also adding a scatter filter so discs stay off the cowl's belly region, keeping to surfaces where the normal faces upward enough. I'm now working out the chin scoop geometry beneath the nose, checking where the octagon's bottom vertex sits relative to the cowl's center height so the scoop box aligns with the actual belly surface rather than floating or clipping through it.

Shaping the scoop loft stations...

I need to check whether the loft supports flat caps, and work out the embedding depth so the scoop sits properly inside the cowl's belly — centering it so the top edge tucks under the bottom edge by about 0.06 units. I also need to account for how the cowl's underside slopes upward near the vertex, since the octagonal cross-section rises at roughly 22.5° away from center, which shifts the effective clearance at the scoop's edges.

I'll set the scoop dimensions across stations, defining front as the mouth with z=2.4 smaller and z=3.2 largest. Then I'm moving to the spinner, planning a lathed shape along the propeller axis starting at the spinner base position.

Writing spinner profile points...

But I realize the backplate (0.8x0.88) is much bigger than the spinner's 0.28 radius, leaving a gap, and the prop hub at z=3.75 would actually sit inside the spinner given its radius there (~0.27) — so the steel hub disc and blade roots would be hidden unless I rework the geometry. I'm considering making the hub disc visible as a short cylinder of radius 0.3 positioned so blades can emerge through slots in the spinner shell.

Since the spinner's radius right there is around 0.235, a flange ring of radius 0.3 and thickness 0.07 works nicely as a visible collar wrapping the spinner. I also want flat caps on the loft so the cowl lip closes cleanly at z=3.5, and I'm weighing whether to add a dark backplate disc behind the spinner for depth.

Now I'm mapping out the blade geometry as a tapered 2D profile in radius/chord coordinates, defining the outline points from the root near the hub out to a rounded tip, with the chord narrowing gradually before rounding off at the blade tip.

Then I need to figure out how to orient this flat profile in 3D: I'm setting up a local basis perpendicular to the propeller axis so I can place each blade at the correct angular position around the hub, using cross products to derive the radial and tangential directions for rotating blades around the shaft.

For the twist, since a single extrude can't vary pitch along the radius easily, I'm simplifying to a uniform tilt per blade—rotating the chord direction slightly toward the axis direction to fake a pitch angle, keeping the local x/y basis roughly orthogonal so the extrusion thickness stays aligned with the blade's intended profile.

I'm now planning to split each blade into three extrude segments with decreasing twist (steeper near the hub, flatter toward the tip), each defined by a quadrilateral outline from leading/trailing edge width functions at the segment boundaries, so I can approximate a twisted blade using straight extrudes stacked along the radius.

I'm defining the width profile with upper and lower chord offsets, adding rounded tip points, and splitting the blade into four radial segments with decreasing pitch angles, giving the tip segment a distinct color. I'm settling on a constant thickness with a small bevel rather than tapering it along the radius.

Now I'm adding a thin leading-edge rod per blade segment using a helper function that positions points along the hub radius and chord offset, computing roughly three rods per blade plus the extrudes, collar, and root hole—about nine parts per blade across all three blades.

For the root, I'm placing a small chalk cylinder at the blade base where it meets the spinner, sizing it so the blade emerges right at the spinner's surface radius, then adding a cuff collar slightly larger around that junction. I'm also planning a thin hub flange cylinder at the mounting position to tie the blades together visually.

Now I'm working out the spinner paper band — a thin ring positioned partway along the spinner's taper, built as a short lathe profile so it reads as a raised collar rather than a flat disc, interpolating the spinner's radius at that point to size it correctly.

Still computing ring geometry...

Adding three meridian seam rods at 60/180/300 degrees along the spinner profile, then considering small studs on the flange ring but deciding to keep it simple with just the steel cylinder rather than adding extra detail there.

I'm adding a thin ring detail at z=3.47 for the cowl lip, plus panel seam loops around z=2.9 and 3.3 to suggest paneling — using small lifted loops swept around the surface, being careful the plane points land inside the cowl region so the loop function doesn't fail.

For the hinged-panel outline, I'm considering using a drape operation on a closed polyline, but worried the sampling is too sparse at corners. I'll instead densify the rectangle path myself with points every 0.05 units so the drape hugs the surface closely, writing a helper to generate those rectangle points along the correct side.

Actually, starting the drape from too far outside the surface risks snapping to the wrong facet, so I should start the sample points closer in, around x=0.45 instead of the surface boundary, then sweep the resulting path with a thin profile and the fuselage bone, coloring the line and rounding the corners afterward. I'm also weighing whether to add a secondary circular hatch or filler cap nearby, but it may be unnecessary clutter given the existing stud rows.

I'll densify points across the rectangle, cast rays from outside toward the surface, lift each hit point slightly along its normal, and build a closed polyline from those points to sweep — deterministic and avoids weirdness. I'll also add a dorsal seam along the cowl's top ridge using downward rays, since it's cheap and worth including as one extra part.

For the exhaust stacks, I'm placing six per side along the fuselage, angled slightly upward and back to mimic the real aircraft's canted mouths, embedding each stack's base slightly into the surface using the hit normal. I'm considering whether to add a thin rim ring around each mouth for extra detail but may skip it to keep things simple.

Still writing stack geometry...

Adding the muzzle hole as a small sphere, then considering a front cowl lip ring and inner deep annulus around the spinner base for extra detail on the nose.

The front face normal lines up with the path tangent, good. I'm adding a middle station at z=2.9 to smooth the loft curve between the two end stations, checking that the lip centers match the computed slope. Confirming the loft orientation keeps width along world X and height along the local up vector, which matches what I want.

Now I'm working out the camouflage sector angles for the cowl surface, deciding where to place patches around the tube's circumference so they align cleanly with the octagonal cross-section's vertex angles, picking symmetric ranges on either side.

Belly gets a wide range from 135 to 225 degrees, and I'm using normal-filtering for scattered discs on upper side facets instead. No joints are needed since parts aren't named for joining, so I'll skip that step and move on to basic vector helpers using THREE.Vector3, trusting the runtime Ctx type even without declaring it explicitly.
